speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: STATEMENT ON TRANSFER OF DUTIES OF MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a statement about the transfer of certain duties from the Minister of Agriculture to the Minister of Forestry, on which some questions were asked yesterday.
It will be recalled that on February 20, in the debate on the address in reply to the throne speech, I described the intention of the government to combine forestry with the work of rural development and to create a ministry of forestry and rural development. By an order in council of March 5, 1964, pursuant to the Public Service Rearrangement and Transfer of Duties Act the powers, duties and functions of the Minister of Agriculture under the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act and the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act were transferred to the Minister of Forestry. The same order in council also transferred to the Minister of Forestry the administration of the program respecting freight assistance and grain storage costs on western feed grain.
I might say, Mr. Speaker, that it has also been decided to establish a special three man executive committee to co-ordinate policies for agriculture. Its chairman is the Minister of Agriculture; the other two members are the Minister of Trade and Commerce, because of his responsibility for grain marketing, and the Minister of Forestry, who is to have responsibility also for rural development and for feed grains moved from western Canada. A bill to establish a ministry of forestry and rural development will be placed before parliament at an early date.
There has been some inquiry as to whether certain other functions of the Minister of Agriculture were to be transferred to the Minister of Forestry. In that connection I should say that an earlier order in council had been made on February 3 but was withdrawn. It did include the Farm Credit Act and the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act among the functions to be transferred to the Minister of Forestry. That order was never proceeded with because it had been prepared before the new Minister of Forestry came into office on February 3. When he was appointed, he and the Minister of Agriculture jointly urged that a precise transfer of functions
864	HOUSE OF
Agriculture Minister Duties Transferred should not be finalized until the new minister had had time to familiarize himself with the problems which would be involved in the establishment of his office.
Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, by the wish of both ministers concerned, the transfer of duties was held in abeyance for a few weeks. The two ministers then agreed as to the duties to be transferred. Their joint recommendation was accepted by me and by the cabinet, and was embodied in the order in council of March 5 to which I have referred.
Yesterday there was a suggestion that the government was in default in not having published the order in council of February 3 and the subsequent order which revoked it. That allegation, Mr. Speaker, is quite unfounded. Strictly speaking, as hon. members know, there is no statutory obligation to publish such orders, but in practice they are tabled in a monthly summary. The list for February will, as a matter of course, include the two orders in question. Meantime people who asked for copies of the above orders, including an alert newspaperman who asked some time ago, were given them in the usual way.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: STATEMENT ON TRANSFER OF DUTIES OF MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make reference to the statement just placed before the house by the Prime Minister. In order to do so I will have to refer to the various orders in council. The changes in the cabinet, as I recall them, were made on February 3. On that date an order in council was passed, P.C. 1964-157, which states, reading only the appropriate portions, that:
... on the recommendation of the Prime Minister, pursuant to the Public Service Rearrangement and Transfer of Duties Act, is pleased hereby to transfer to the Minister of Forestry the powers, duties or functions of the Minister of Agriculture under the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act, the Farm Credit Act, the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act, and the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, and in respect of the administration of the program respecting freight assistance and grain storage...
His Excellency.. .is hereby further pleased to designate the Minister of Forestry, as the appropriate minister, for the purposes of the Financial Administration Act, with respect to the Farm Credit Corporation.
That order in council came into effect and could not be changed by the wish of the government without another order in council. In other words it continued in effect until a change of heart took place on the part of the government on February 20, so that for 17 days the Minister of Agriculture was divested of these powers and they were transferred to the Minister of Forestry.
It is of interest to ask, and I would ask the Prime Minister to advise, whether during


that period of time the Minister of Agriculture discharged the duties of these departments which had been transferred from him; because the fact is that if anything other than purely administrative work was done it was done illegally. For 17 days the Minister of Agriculture was a minister without these powers. Then on February 20 His Excellency, on the recommendation of the Prime Minister, revoked the order in council. I ask specifically what happened during those 17 days when the Minister of Agriculture was outside the veil.
Then on March 5, as the Prime Minister said, another order in council was passed whereby certain powers were transferred back to the Minister of Agriculture under ARDA and the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act, and in respect of freight rates. This is a strange and peculiar performance to transfer powers away from a minister and then, at the end of 17 days, find out that they should not have been transferred away.
What happened during those 17 days? Were these particular powers auctioned off as between two ministers? Certainly never before has there been an auction sale of powers on the part of ministers.
Stripped as the minister was of these prerogatives, I ask who exercised the powers between the 3rd and the 20th? The minister is not here today so that we could have asked him some questions in this regard, but is it a fact that there was great difficulty in the cabinet? Is it a fact, as stated outside the house, I am informed, that there was a threat on the part of the Minister of Agriculture that unless these powers came back to him he would go? These are all questions that arise.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: STATEMENT ON TRANSFER OF DUTIES OF MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the questions that were asked yesterday we naturally welcome the fact that the Prime Minister, without further delay, has made a statement on the issues involved, and I appreciate the fact that he has made it on motions so that brief comments can be made on it.
The first comment I wish to make is that it seems very strange that an order in council transferring duties from one minister to another, was made-as the Prime Minister implied-without adequate consultation with the ministers concerned before it was done.
The second point I wish to make is in fact one that the Leader of the Opposition has commented on, and I make it very precisely; that once an order in council has been passed, if it is a proper order in council based on a statute it has the force of law and no one, not even a minister of the crown, has the right to agree to vary that order or to agree to disregard it. Therefore any actions between
MARCH 13, 1964	8B5
February 3 and February 20 on the part of either or both of the ministers concerned, that were not in accordance with the order in council of February 3, were contrary to the law.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am not trying to blow this into an issue of the proportions of the flour milling report of 1949, or some other things that have happened, but if the rule of law means anything it applies to the government as much as it does to the ordinary citizens of the country. If two ministers choose by arrangement between themselves, with the consent of the rest of the cabinet, to disregard the law, then that is breaking the law just as much as when any citizen breaks any law of the land.
The other comment I wish to make is that the Prime Minister cannot brush aside the law regarding the publishing in the Canada Gazette of orders in council. He says that an alert newspaperman learned about these orders in council. Well, all power to him. I may also say that the privy council office this morning did not hesitate to agree to send to me, when I asked for them over the telephone, copies of the orders in council of February 3 and February 20. Neither did the privy council office hesitate for a moment to answer the question I put to that office: "Have these orders in council been published in the Canada Gazette?" The clear and forthright answer was "Not yet". Of course I did not need to ask that question because I knew the answer. However, I have in my hand the Canada Gazette, part 2, for February 12 and February 26. The next issue, of course, will not come out until a date in March. It is quite clear that the order in council of February 3 was not published in the Canada Gazette within 30 days of the time it was made.
The Prime Minister says there is no legal requirement but that it is only a matter of practice or tradition. I remind him that there is a very precise legal requirement. It is section 6, subsection 1, of the Regulations Act, which is chapter 235 of the Revised Statutes of Canada. 1952. It is very brief. Let me read it to the Prime Minister and to all who are concerned.
Every regulation shall be published in English and in French in the Canada Gazette within 30 days alter it is made.
There is no escape from that whatsoever except section 9, subsection 2, which does give the governor in council the power to make another order in council exempting some other order from publication. If there was such an order in council it would have to be published, but from the fact that the orders of February 3 and February 20 are available to the press and are available to
Agriculture Minister Duties Transferred us as members of parliament it is clear that there has not been an order in council making these two orders in council secret.
It is quite clear that the government has changed its mind. It is quite clear that the government has decided that what was proposed in the order in council of February 3 it did not want to carry out. It has the right to do that. The transfer of duties prerogative can be used to push ministers around as much as the government wishes. But the government is just as much bound by law as is parliament, just as much bound by law as the people of Canada.
Although this may seem to be a small matter, the plain fact is that my allegation of yesterday stands up, for the Prime Minister now admits that the order in council was passed on February 3. Today is March 13, Friday the 13th in fact, and not yet has that order in council been published in the Canada Gazette. Even if it is published now, this still does not carry out the strict requirement of the law that it shall be published in the Canada Gazette within 30 days after it is made.
What is strange about our parliamentary system is that there does not seem to be any penalty, other than criticism or lack of confidence and public dismay, when the government breaks the law. We had this in 1949 'when Hon. Stuart Garson broke the law requiring him to table a certain report under the Combines Investigation Act. We have had other instances, but I cite that one as a clear example. There seems to be nothing than can be done by way of penalty when the government breaks the law. I know of no penalty that can be imposed on the government for having broken this law; but if we are going to establish respect for the law in this country, if we are going to insist that it means something, I suggest that respect for the law should be practised without any question by the government itself.

speechtext:
Perhaps I could deal with the requirement under the law which the hon. gentleman has stated has been broken by this government. This is what is required under the law; first, publication of orders, which means publication in the Canada Gazette, as governed by the requirements of the Regulations Act or in specific instances by requirement indicated in other pieces of legislation which authorize an order in council for a particular purpose. There is no requirement for publication of orders like those now in question, either under the Regulations Act or under the Public Service Rearrangement and Transfer of Duties Act, which was the authorizing statute in this case.
Apart from publication in the Canada Gazette, orders may also be made public by tabling in parliament. Such tabling is sometimes required by a particular act and is sometimes done voluntarily by the minister directly concerned for special reasons. Again, there is no requirement in the Rearrangement and Transfer of Duties Act to table orders of the type involved here. It is the practice of the privy council office, Mr. Speaker, to table a monthly summary of the orders in council, not as the result of any statutory requirement but under a standing arrangement initiated by my predecessor, Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent. This summary lists the orders in council by subject and date of approval, but without giving the privy council number. The two orders in question about which we have been talking this morning were both approved in February and would, as a matter of course, be included in the summary for that month, which has not yet been published or tabled.

I rise on a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker. The Prime Minister has sought to set aside the section of the Regulations Act which I read by the assertion he made that it does not apply. I will not enter into a lengthy argument; I will simply read, for his benefit, a portion of the interpretation section of the Regulations Act. It says;
In this act,
(a) "regulation" means a rule, order, regulation, by-law or proclamation
(1) made, in the exercise of a legislative power conferred by or under an act of parliament, by the governor in council-
An order in council is something passed by the governor in council under the authority of an act of parliament. I submit this is clearly covered by the act and therefore is subject to the requirements of section 6, subsection 1, which I have already read.

speechtext:
First of all I assure you, Mr. Speaker, and the house that I do not propose to enter into the debate that has been carried on for some time now, nor is it my intention to discuss the matter from a legal point of view as members have been doing. However, I should like to avail myself of the opportunity afforded by custom to make a few observations on the statement made by the Prime Minister.
First of all, we appreciate this statement and we do hope that it will have the effect of clearing up a great deal of the uncertainty that has accumulated as a result of statements that have been made and decisions that have been taken and announced by the government. I must say that while all this juggling of responsibility has been going on between ministers, the farmers of eastern Canada in particular have been awaiting with impatience a solution to some of their problems. We do hope that now some of these uncertainties have been removed, these problems will be resolved.
We believe there must be a correlation of the various agricultural policies now in force in order that agriculture may receive the full benefit of these policies. Reference has been made to P.F.R.A., to the ARDA program, to the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act, and so on. We have insisted that there should be nation-wide policies with adaptation to suit particular areas as may be required. We hope, therefore, that the changes announced this morning may result in a more

uniform and effective administration of agricultural policy both in eastern and in western Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I have no intention of taking up too much time on the first item of the supplementary budget, which relates to agriculture. Yet, I would like to ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) to consider a matter which we think particularly important.
Mr. Chairman, in the field of agriculture, and more particularly with regard to the federal Farm Credit Corporation, there is, at this time, a certain lack of administration, organization or adjustment of the legislation to the prevailing conditions in the province of Quebec.
Mr. Chairman, it is incredible how many farmers in the province of Quebec-I have witnessed it everyday in the riding of Lapointe-have had their application for a loan to the federal Farm Credit Corporation rejected. This is due to the fact that the act in its present form is not adjusted to existing circumstances and farming conditions in the province of Quebec. The legislation was enacted for the western farmer for whom it works out very well but not for the eastern farmer.
On the other hand, the organization and administration of the corporation are not sufficiently developed to help the credit inspectors or advisers study every application and see to it that loans are granted in the majority of cases in the province of Quebec.
We have now been sitting for two years in the house dealing with the problem, telling the government again and again that the federal Farm Credit Corporation in the province of Quebec has not been sufficiently developed from an administrative and organizational point of view and is insufficiently adjusted to circumstances.
It must be recognized that there has been some progress, Mr. Chairman. We must admit, for instance, that in our district of Lake St. John, there was only one credit counselor in four counties; moreover, that one credit counsellor came from Quebec for half a day or one day a month. Now, at that time, in

Saskatchewan, Manitoba or Alberta, there were four credit counsellors in each federal riding.
We had one for four constituencies, who came one day each month, whereas, in the western provinces, there were four credit consultants by constituency, and on a fulltime basis.
Things have improved. At present, we have two credit consultants for the four constituencies. However, with two credit consultants for the four constituencies, we are still far away from the average prevailing in western Canada, where there are four consultants per constituency.
Mr. Chairman, I feel that the Minister of Finance-since he seems to have been chosen to jot down any remarks we may wish to make-should speak to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays), who, unfortunately, is not here, and to the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve), who is supposed to look after such matters in the province of Quebec, to inform them of the need to increase our representation in this respect as compared to that existing in western Canada, and in order to try to promote farmers' loans in the province of Quebec. There is a tremendous shortage of such consultants. We do not have the same ratio of credit consultants as the western provinces. And we are entitled to have enough credit consultants to meet the requests for agricultural loans made by farmers in the province of Quebec.
Moreover, the act should be adapted to prevailing conditions.
In western Canada, the average amount of the loans is much higher and they are much easier to get. Why? Because the law has foreseen the conditions and circumstances in that part of the country where wheat is grown on 1,000 acres of land. On the other hand, farms have only 100 acres on the average, in the province of Quebec. Since that is sufficient to raise cattle, 100 acres are enough for a farmer; he does not need 1,000 acres.
Because he has less land, he has less real estate to put up as a guarantee; however, even if he has less square feet or square inches to till with a substantial farm loan the Quebec farmer can produce just as much as a western farmer who has a much greater wheat acreage.
The Farm Credit Act has no provision for these circumstances. In my opinion, the Minister of Finance, who is now responsible for the financial aspect of this problem, should advise the Minister of Agriculture to change this situation.
It is true that there has been improvement in that field these last two years. In my own riding of Lapointe, more farm loans were
Supply-A griculture
granted to farmers in 1963 than in 1962, and much more than in 1961. I readily recognize the efforts of the government along those lines. However, there still are serious inadequacies in the act, because too many farmers tell us: the corporation refused to grant us a loan, we have to leave our farms and go to the city to live on social assistance.
That is why we witness at present in our ridings a mass departure from the country to the city, which must be checked because, everyone agrees, the rural class, and especially the farming community, is still the most stable class in our society and the foundation of our country.
Mr. Chairman, it is for those reasons that I-and I do so without partisanship, and I give credit to the present government for its action in that direction over the last two years-suggest that the agricultural field is perhaps the most important one at this time and that it is imperative that constant efforts be made in order to step up those already achieved in that direction, in order to assist our farmers.
I trust that the Minister of Finance will take our suggestions into consideration and act upon them.

I fear that the pattern under which assistance is provided to marginal centres tends to intensify the lack of interest now prevailing within the Department of Agriculture which is responsible for extending farm services to French Canada. Now, that important department, supported by public funds, which has the duty to serve the whole farm population, be it French or English, does not appear lately to be interested in improving its relations with French Canadians who nevertheless constitute 30 per cent of the farmers in Canada. The province of Quebec alone, through its agriculture, provides Canada annually with more than $500 million in revenue.
The Department of Agriculture has an important part to play in the Canadian nation. Its purpose is to give instructions in agricultural matters everywhere in Canada, since agriculture is not practised within the department itself but indeed on every farm in this country. The department is supposed to play its part as leader and to assist the farmers.
Thirty per cent of the farmers are French speaking, and most of them are unilingual. According to the constitution, they have a right to be French and they must, like all other citizens, contribute to the support of the department which, in turn, has the responsibility of assisting them just the same as English speaking farmers.
English speaking farmers are generally very well served by the federal Department of Agriculture, but it has been altogether different for some time as regards French speaking farmers.
The federal Department of Agriculture uses the services of translators and interpreters in their transactions with French speaking farmers, as they have no other means of direct communication with the senior officers of the department who are not bilingual. Moreover, it does not seem likely that this situation will be improved, since it tends, lately, to get worse.

Mr. Chairman, the situation of our eastern farmers is precarious. Their income is decreasing in an alarming way and it is therefore essential, to my mind, to improve the means of communication between French speaking farmers and the federal Department of Agriculture, so that they may seek information, here in Ottawa, to improve their economic position.
Let me tell you what is the situation in the department at the present time.
First of all, it seems that no French Canadian officials are wanted in higher positions in the Department of Agriculture.
Second, the few French Canadian officials who occupy ordinary positions do not get promotions.
Third, promotions seem to be tolerated only in the "Quebec reserve", because good care is taken not to let any qualified agronomist come to headquarters in Ottawa. As you know, Mr. Chairman, several French speaking agronomists have their doctor's or master's degree in agricultural science, and are graduates from large American universities.
In the fourth place, the federal Department of Agriculture is now trying to keep up appearances by publishing press releases on bilingualism, which does not mean anything, to my mind. Indeed, we might well wonder whether promotions in the federal Department of Agriculture have been awarded to a few French speaking agronomists or technicians in the last eight months, or whether there has been some discrimination with regard to acceptable bilingual candidates.
I know for a fact that the former minister of agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) and the former prime minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) made the necessary efforts to improve the situation, and everybody knows that Mr. Chagnon, who was assistant deputy minister, under a decision of the former government, was appointed associate deputy minister of agriculture with authority to share in all responsibilities and decisions of the federal Department of Agriculture. But the administration was defeated, and the situation remained in abeyance.
It would be interesting to know how things are going, presently, in that important Department of Agriculture, which now is in danger of not serving anymore agriculture in eastern Canada, since the government changed its promise into a department of forestry and rural development.
I strongly suggest an inquiry be immediately conducted in that department, where

it would appear they are not too interested in serving eastern Canada farmers, and especially French speaking farmers.
The present government appointed a special commission to study the situation concerning bilingualism in Canada. That commission has been sitting for two months already, and it is still trying to define its terms of reference.
Consequently, it would be wise if that commission had the responsibility and the duty of having inequities removed where they exist. I suggest there are inequities at the present time in the Department of Agriculture and I request the commissioners to make a full and thorough inquiry into that department.
Mr. Chairman, in closing, I wish to bring out some concrete facts concerning the personnel of the Department of Agriculture of Canada.
Out of 542 upper echelon employees at headquarters in Ottawa and Hull, 6.5 per cent are bilingual.
It should be pointed out, however, that, if I am not mistaken, no bilingual person is to be found holding a job paying $12,000 or over, with the exception of the associate deputy minister, who has been side-tracked and is no longer part of the team running the Department of Agriculture. And that, in spite of the representations and efforts on our part, for it is through a decision of the previous government that Mr. Chagnon was appointed associate deputy minister.
Among those holding positions of lesser importance, the majority cannot do their work in their own language, because they do not have bilingual secretaries at their disposal, and that even goes for the few who have to deal with the province of Quebec.

I think it is appropriate to say something at this time with respect to the item under agriculture now being discussed. Since the item deals with general administration and as there is a particular item farther down dealing with farm credit I think my remarks are germane at this point. Frankly, Mr. Chairman, I am most concerned about the legality of the action taken by the government with regard to those sections of the Department of Agriculture involved in the order in council of the 3rd of February. These are the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act, the Farm Credit Act, the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act, the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and the Farm Credit Corporation. It will be recalled that an order in council was passed on the 3rd of February transferring these activities from the authority of the Minister of Agriculture to that of the

Minister of Forestry. On the 20th of February another order in council was passed which simply revoked the previous one.
The question is: What is the position of the government with respect to that fatal 17 days? There would be no doubt if the government had passed another order in council transferring these branches back to the authority of the Minister of Agriculture, but the government, with its well known reputation for action, plunged in somewhat hastily -and almost surreptitiously, as far as the public is concerned-on the 3rd of February. They did not even bother to publish what they were doing, and some of us have serious doubts as to the knowledge of the Minister of Agriculture with regard to what the government did on that day. I think perhaps our suspicions that there was a period of 17 days which elapsed are strengthened by our knowledge of the Minister of Agriculture. Certainly, in the light of his other duties as auctioneer, we can easily imagine 17 days going by before he returned to his office to find he had been bereft of most of his responsibilities.
I must say that the corrective action taken by the government on February 20 bears the stamp of the usual action taken by this administration when it finds it has acted unwisely or hastily without regard for the pertinent questions that must be considered when a change as fundamental as this is made. The administration acts in haste and retreats in even greater haste. When the retreat bears all the indications of a rout, and when they suddenly find their fingers burned, they usually retreat in such haste they forget what they are doing, or what they must do to protect their rear. They do not know what kind of a shambles they have left behind them. They just move back fast, say nothing, and hope they will get away with it.
The situation which faces us at the moment is that the government is asking us to vote supplementary estimates covering some items upon which action undoubtedly was taken during the period of time in which no one had any legal authority to act. As a matter of fact, departmental officials who may have been under ministerial authority did not, in fact, have any legal authorization to make expenditures under these votes. In other words, Mr. Chairman, I think the government probably spent money illegally. If we were to pass these items now, the parliament of Canada would be approving the illegality of these actions. I cannot see how the minister or the government can ask this parliament to pass quickly the Department of Agriculture items until they have indicated at what date they intend to introduce legislation to make legal these illegal actions, which were taken between February 3 and February 20.

I do not want to labour the point because I do not pretend to be a legal authority. However, I have had the benefit of some conversations with other lawyers whose opinions I value highly and, quite simply, in these circumstances, there would have been no doubt if the second order in council had just reversed the first one and restored these items. Certainly one wonders why it was done in this manner. The point raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre concerning the failure to publish in the Canada Gazette certainly assumes new significance when we consider the awkward position in which the government is now. I suggest that perhaps the ministers of the cabinet disagreed, perhaps there was fighting in their own ranks, and I suggest that this action on February 3 was sneaky. They wanted to avoid throwing the light of public opinion on their actions, and therefore did not publish these orders as they were required to do. When they found they were in hot water on February 20 and had to restore these items, they were more than grateful at that time that no one knew about it.
I do not believe I am inaccurate when I describe the actions of the government in this case as rather sneaky, underhanded, precipitate, hasty, ill-considered, illogical, wrong and stupid. I hope that before the government decides to ask the pity of this parliament, to ask our assistance in trying to get them out of this muddle, they will give us the reassurance, as the first sign of penitence, that they intend to take remedial action to clear up this illegal situation. Perhaps before we are asked to give further consideration to these supplementary estimates the minister will tell us how quickly the government will be able to bring in a remedial bill. I suggest this should be the first step before any further progress is made in voting money which, according to indications, has been spent illegally.

May I add a word to the discussion on the Department of Agriculture? I shall be very brief. I would urge the Department of Agriculture to give consideration to this question of the time it takes to administer farm credit, particularly in the province of Ontario. I have a lot of material here and could speak at length on this subject, but I think it is sufficient to draw the attention of the minister to question No. 120 reported on page 532 of Hansard. The question reads:
What is the average length of time taken be* tween the receipts of application and the dispersals of moneys in the cases of the last 50 agricultural loans in Ontario processed through the Farm Credit Corporation?
The answer to that question, sir, was 209 days. I do not believe this is good enough.

Supply-Agriculture
This answer indicates that, somehow or other, there has been a breakdown in the administration. The second question is:
What is the actual time taken in the case of the ten slowest of these loans-
The answer is 430 days for Norfolk; 408 days for Lanark; 377 days for Prescott, and so on. The third question was:
What are the dates of receipt of application in the cases of the ten oldest loans in Ontario still in the course of being processed by the Farm Credit Corporation-
The answer to that question shows that we have loans being processed from the 15th of November, 1961, in Grey; the 28th of February, 1962, in Halton; the 12th of March, 1962, in Leeds and so on. I could go on at greater length but I believe that if the minister and some of his assistants will now take a careful look at this problem as it relates to these areas of Ontario where there is a land registry system as distinct from the Torrens system, it will be seen that our farm credit administration has actually broken down. It is not proper to make our farmers wait for 300 days to get a loan from the government. I believe most people who have had some experience in this matter will tell you that a loan can be processed in approximately two or three weeks through a trust company. It does not sound reasonable to me that it should take upwards of a year to process a loan for a farmer when the land, in some instances, has been held by his family for a very long time. I am sure, sir, that the process can be streamlined. Perhaps we should look at the Veterans Land Act legislation under which I am sure things are moving more rapidly.
Another factor in connection with this problem is the remuneration of the legal agent. It is really not sufficient for the amount of work they are asked to do. In some places in Ontario there are legal agents who do not want to touch this business at all, and not entirely because of the monetary return. Many of these people would be quite happy to give the services of their legal offices at even less money.
The trouble is that doing work for the Farm Credit Corporation, with files going from one office to another and taking orders, in this particular case, from Toronto, really means that each agent's law office is getting a particularly bad name. That is not a situation which has been brought about by this administration-I do not think even by the previous government. It is just something which, like Topsy, has grown and developed. It is about time we took a close look at this and streamlined this operation because if we did it would mean a great deal to the usefulness of farm credit in Ontario.

I do not intend to make any extended remarks on this item. I would prefer to make my general comments on the estimates of the Department of Agriculture in the presence of the minister. But I do think the point raised by my hon. friend from Edmonton-Strathcona is one which should be taken into consideration by the minister. I noticed that when my hon. friend was speaking, the minister was engaged in a discussion with his neighbour and did not appear to be listening too closely. For this reason, I wish to repeat what was said. The point he was raising dealt with the orders in council passed on February 3 and February 20, the first authorizing the transfer of certain powers from the Department of Agriculture to the Department of Forestry, and the second simply revoking the order which was passed on February 3. The point here is that as far as I can see there is no authority given for the Minister of Forestry to act with respect to the departments which were involved, so any payments of money which were authorized or any directives which were given by the Minister of Forestry concerning those particular branches of the Department of Agriculture were illegal.
This is the point upon which we would like the government to comment. There should have been an order in council which transferred back to the Department of Agriculture those branches of the department which were taken away, and I wonder if the minister or his officials could give us an explanation before we pass this item. We certainly do not want this committee placed in a position of voting money which has been spent illegally. I think this is an important point which should be cleared up at this time.

speechtext: I shall be glad to answer that particular question. The government is certainly not disintegrating and there is no split in the cabinet whatever. Of course, I understand that the hon. gentleman may know about that sort of thing.

I only want to say a word about this. I think is is a very important subject and that the legal people should give more consideration to this than they appear to have done on the government benches. I say this because this problem was raised, first, in the Family Herald and has caused a great deal of concern among farm people across the country. I think they will be looking forward to hearing a statement on the points raised by my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre as to the legality of the action which the government has taken. I think it is imperative that the government should reach a decision of some kind and that the committee should not be left up in the air.
Certainly, in discussing the estimates affecting an item of administration, we are bound to express some concern because, I am sure, there has been a complete lack of morale within the Department of Agriculture since this government took over.
Hear, hear.

You can give credit to the minister of agriculture in the former administration for his ability in knowing what agriculture is. Supporters of the previous government are going to take it, anyway. This government has given slavish adherence to the practice established over the years, namely that the Minister of Agriculture should be from western Canada and that a dummy minister is better than having one from anywhere else in Canada. This has caused the trouble. We do not know what to take away from the department, or what to keep, because the minister has not shown any great ability in any field. It might have been wise to get rid of him, as apparently the Prime Minister intended to do. He

Supply-Agriculture
thought the matter over and said, in the third week of January, "We are going to abolish the Department of Agriculture and have a new department comprised of forestry and agriculture". He later found this was not quite so easy because a great many people are still interested in agriculture and there are aspects of the department that cannot very well be administered in conjunction with the Department of Forestry. I think that we in this house have a right to know what the thinking of the government is going to be, not in terms of this order in council or other orders in council, but in terms of what is going to happen to this department, before we are asked to give our approval to an estimate covering the administration of the department. Things could not be worse in the Department of Agriculture if you wanted them to be. The only way the situation could be further confused,
I think, would be in a legal sense, because I am sure the morale of most of the people in this department is very, very low.
I am not going to add to the remarks of the hon. member for Leeds who spoke about farm credit. The Farm Credit Corporation has been kicked around a number of times over the past two or three years. Under the former Liberal government and the old farm loan board, things had got into a very disgraceful condition. This program was opposed by almost everyone who had ever had anything to do with the farm loan board. Then, because of the advantages that were given to veterans under the V.L.A., the Farm Credit Corporation as we know it today was built and designed on the basis of supplying to all agriculture the benefits that had accrued from the legislation peculiar to veterans.
I doubt whether anybody in the Department of Agriculture now knows where they are going. They may be concerned with rehabilitation; they may have something to do with rural development; they may be concerned with agriculture; they may also be concerned with forestry. Therefore there must be a great deal of confusion in that department. This is certainly a branch of the department that deserves consideration, because the method of granting loans based on land values has not really met the problem in many parts of the country. This was mentioned by the hon. member for Lapointe this morning. With reference to those lands upon which are grown crops that require a large area, the basis is not unreasonable; but in those areas which grow highly specialized and highly developed crops, the land values very seldom, if ever, bear a straight relationship to the amount of money necessary to provide an economic unit. Choose any of the

problems connected with the Department of Agriculture and I am sure you will find a farmer who will say, "I wish somebody would do something", with regard to some of these particular problems. It may be there is a closer liaison with some of the farm organizations than there is with members of parliament, because I was surprised that when the Canadian federation of agriculture visited us this year they were not the least concerned about the fact that the Department of Agriculture might disappear; and they have not yet raised this matter. Well, perhaps they had been given more information than the rest of us. Perhaps they knew there would be further developments and considered there was no point in making a decision on this question when the position might change in the next few weeks.
If the minister of any of these three departments which are today involved in agriculture would really sit down and do something for agriculture we would be very satisfied. This problem has come about because of the inability of the Liberal party to adapt themselves to the face that they would have to have an eastern agricultural minister. With regard to who should be the eastern minister of this department, I could name two or three of the young fellows of the Liberal party who are interested in agriculture, are actually engaged in agriculture, are people who know how to farm, who know what are some of the problems of eastern agriculture and also have the education to enable them to understand the problems of agriculture in western Canada. I am shocked when I find the Prime Minister playing around when we so desperately need good material in the Department of Agriculture. I believe the Prime Minister has available a number of people capable of dealing with this matter. I suggest that those he has played around with so far are not suitable in the opinion of most Canadian people, and in my opinion they are not equipped to solve the problems which face agriculture.
I think it is very unwise for us to be dealing with the final supplementary estimates of this department when the minister is not here to explain to us what the government intends to do with the department. Unless we know what is really asked of us and what the government intends, we should not be asked to support anything. I say this because I am confused as to what we are asked to support. Parliament is confused; I am sure that at least the cabinet is confused, and the Canadian people are as confused as anyone. I think it is downright unfair to ask us to approve the final estimates of 1963-64 on the question of agriculture while the whole situation is so confused. I believe

the Minister of Finance-for whom I have considerable respect-would be very well advised to stand this item and wait until the Minister of Agriculture has a chance to look at it, when it could then be referred back to the committee for approval.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few brief remarks on the estimates of the Department of Agriculture. I fully agree with my colleagues who said a while ago that it is absolutely impossible for us to adopt those estimates as long as we are denied an explanation concerning the situation which exists within the Department of Agriculture.
Before April 8, 1963, the cabinet included a full-time minister of agriculture and a fulltime minister of forestry. The minister of agriculture also had two parliamentary secretaries. However, only one minister of agriculture and one parliamentary secretary were appointed after the election of April 8 last. On May 20, 1963, the government put on the order paper a motion to the effect that it would appoint a minister of agriculture for eastern Canada and a minister of agriculture for western Canada.
All through the last session, we waited impatiently for the government to do something in that connection. When we asked questions, we were told that, in order to solve the problems of agriculture in the eastern part of the country, the resolution would have to be passed so as to enable the incumbent, who was then minister without portfolio, to become minister of agriculture for eastern Canada.
We noticed at the end of the session that the government had to withdraw, to retreat, and we witnessed the migration of the minister without portfolio to the Department of Citizenship and Immigration.
Afterwards, last February, they stated that they were going to change their procedure, that they would appoint a minister of forestry who later on would become minister of rural development. But care was taken beforehand to take away from the Minister of Agriculture certain responsibilities such as the Canadian wheat board. But we were unaware last February, that other responsibilities had been taken away from the Minister of Agriculture; we learned of it only recently.
Here is the present situation; We have an invisible minister of agriculture. We do not have a parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Agriculture; we have only half a parliamentary secretary, whereas we had two before April 8 last.
Supply-Agriculture
Two were needed to do the work of one.
There was Mr. Pigeon.

Farmers are wondering what the situation will be in a few months and what the Liberal government has in mind regarding the farm policy for eastern Canada and the rest of the country.
Before agreeing to vote the supplementary estimates of the Department of Agriculture, it is the duty of every member of the official opposition to see to it that the situation is clarified. That is why we shall refuse to vote those estimates as long as one of the two so-called ministers of agriculture will not give us some information, will not tell us what he feels bound to do for agriculture in Canada, and what are his responsibilities within the federal government.
Mr. Chairman, until we obtain some explanations from one of those ministers, or from the Prime Minister himself, we shall not be able to vote the supplementary estimates of the Department of Agriculture.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to see this item pass until we receive some answers to some of the questions which have been raised. I notice in the supplementary estimates that the only item with reference to forestry is an expenditure of $91,000. We have often heard remarks coming from the government side, Mr. Chairman, to the effect that we are wasting time. We will not waste any more time if we can get these questions answered. Surely this is the time when we, the elected representatives, have the right, especially when dealing with expenditure of money, to receive answers to our questions.
Where are the ministers concerned? Why are not the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Forestry here? Where are they

when problems such as this are before the committee at the present time? Surely they must have known that these matters would be raised. I see that even the Minister of Finance has gone out. The government have had ample evidence, both from questions asked yesterday and today, that we required answers. Mr. Chairman, I merely want to add some words to what has already been said. Mr. Chairman, naturally no one could deny the President of the Privy Council the opportunity of a few minutes consideration, and the committee will wait with anticipation to hear the explanation which will be made by him. Certainly the Minister of Agriculture, one would have thought, would have been here today. We know he is a busy man, but the Minister of Forestry is not as busy a man as

is the Minister of Agriculture. Perhaps it is a strange coincidence-I am sure it is a coincidence-that these two ministers are away today. They knew that this matter would come up because it was discussed yesterday. They were forewarned. There is nothing more important than the preservation of the rights of parliament in regard to the expenditure of money. I think the house in general will agree with that. Just a moment ago I brought it to the attention of the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance that one of his family name is recognized as a great authority on the subject of the control by parliament of expenditures. I sent the book in question over to him, "Treasury Control", by Samuel H. Beer.
It was published at Oxford University in 1956, and knowing that the parliamentary secretary in his position is a student of the controls that must be exercised over expenditures, I am sure the book is known to him and that the principles contained in it will be carried into effect so far as he is able to do that.

We are asked, Mr. Chairman, to support supplementary estimates of $127,343,000. There is no doubt whatever that the government made an awful mess when it decided to divest the Minister of Agriculture of certain of his powers. There was a long while when the hon. gentleman who is now the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration stood in the shadow of greatness. He was expectant. He was the authority on agriculture. He was going to bring about the dawn of a new day for agriculture in eastern Canada.
There were going to be two ministers. Thej were going to bifurcate the department. Thai went on for a long while, and it was not because of any intention on his part but he

even had the documents issued indicating he was minister of agriculture. Now it has turned out that he was wrong. The great qualifications for agriculture that he possesses are now being lost by his appointment as Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. I can well understand his feelings. He must be awfully disappointed with all that background of agricultural knowledge lost to Canada. And what have they substituted in place of it? They have substituted the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Sauve) as Minister of Forestry.
Then there was not enough work for him so the government decided that some changes should be made. It was one of the most preposterous things that ever took place in this country. I wondered for a while why it was that the Minister of Agriculture was usually in his seat in the house following that episode. Well, what a picture. They stripped him of ARDA, and I can well understand that. He did not know anything about it. They stripped him of the Farm Credit Act. I would like to have heard the discussion that took place in the cabinet if he was present, but I am beginning to wonder if the Minister of Agriculture was there because I am sure he would have been strongly antagonistic to being left almost naked of authority. It was a most unusual thing.

subsubtopic: PROCEDURE TO ESTABLISH PEACE KEEPING FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government expects to hear shortly that a United Nations force will have been constituted for peace keeping duties in Cyprus, with at least two member states contributing forces in addition to those of the three guarantor states, Great Britain, Greece and Turkey. This development comes when the information we are receiving emphasizes the great importance of United Nations intervention at a time of deterioration in the situation.
If this announcement is received from New York before 6 p.m. I shall ask for unanimous consent for the house to consider this afternoon and this evening, if necessary, a resolution approving Canadian participation in the United Nations peace keeping force in the manner described in the resolution. In any event, Mr. Speaker, the resolution will be placed on the order paper so that it can be discussed on Monday if no word is received from New York today.
It is also proposed, Mr. Speaker, that an R.C.A.F. plane should take off this afternoon for Cyprus with a small party of officers.


They will report to the United Nations military representative in Cyprus, General Gyani, and secure from him information about facilities and administrative arrangements in Cyprus for the Canadian United Nations contingent if and when one goes forward. This will be purely a reconnaissance and fact finding mission to expedite and facilitate later moves that may have to be made.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposiiion):
subsubtopic: PROCEDURE TO ESTABLISH PEACE KEEPING FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as far as we in the official opposition are concerned we said this morning that we would co-operate in giving consent to the calling of any such item as is contemplated by the government or is requisite. Certainly this is a serious step. If Canadian troops embark upon this adventure they do so on a dangerous mission, having regard to the words used by the Prime Minister that the situation is deteriorating in Cyprus.
If forces are sent by the United Nations it will be the first time to my knowledge that the United Nations will be taking part in keeping the peace in a situation of civil war. It will also be the first time that the peace force within the United Nations will be one that is brought together and mobilized from among those nations which are prepared not only to provide their blood should there be hostilities but also their treasure. It is one of those things that leads one to wonder whether this step, while necessary, will not in fact weaken the purposes of the United Nations. By that I mean that the United Nations is not operating as an organization in furnishing the membership of the peace keeping force, but members of the United Nations, willing to serve, are being placed in the position where only their voluntary service and their voluntary contribution to the costs make possible the carrying out of the objective of the United Nations.
This is a matter that is particularly important in view of the failure of the U.S.S.R. to make its contribution to the peace keeping operations of the United Nations. As at the first of the year that country was in default some $52,600,000, while France was in default some $16 million for the Congo force, Nationalist China some $10,820,000 for the Congo force, and other nations are in default as well.
Whatever the desirability and the necessity of this action being taken, I am concerned with the effect upon the life and prestige and authority of the United Nations in the years ahead. Certainly the mobilization from

amongst United Nations members of an international force is a long way off when, in the face of so serious a matter as prevails on Cyprus, we have been unable, with all the power and authority of Mr. U Thant and other members of the United Nations, to secure a force which would be paid for by the United Nations rather than by those nations which voluntarily assumed their responsibility and who regard the matter so seriously as to be prepared to make a national sacrifice rather than endanger the peace of the world by refusal to act.

subsubtopic: PROCEDURE TO ESTABLISH PEACE KEEPING FORCE
speechtext:
The members of this group, Mr. Speaker, will certainly co-operate with other members in the house in expediting any motion which the Prime Minister cares to introduce either tonight or tomorrow, if that is necessary in order that parliament may deal with the matter of sending a contribution to the United Nations peace keeping force in Cyprus. This is not the time to discuss that question. I presume we will discuss it more fully when the Prime Minister introduce his motion.
We are all aware of the fact that this will be a hazardous undertaking. It is somewhat unusual that an intervention into a civil war is necessary, but the United Nations has already intervened in what was virtually a civil war in the Congo. Most members will agree that action was necessary at that time to prevent the spread of war and unrest throughout Africa. I think that if the experience of the last few days helps to convince the members of the United Nations of the need for a permanent stand-by peace keeping force that will be available at any time, then recent events will have served a good purpose. I hope that in the future the United Nations will be able to act more expeditiously and not have to wait until members do either what Canada is doing, namely pay for her own peace keeping force, or pass the hat around amongst other nations asking for voluntary contributions. I hope the day will come speedily when the United Nations will act to have a permanent peace keeping force on call and that Canada will make its contribution to such a force. This is something we can discuss later.
The Prime Minister has informed us that a group of officers will be sent some time today in order to ascertain what facilities will be available for a Canadian contingent, if it is to be sent. I certainly agree with the advisability of sending these officers because a good deal of preliminary work will have to be done if this force is to be sent and is to be comfortable, so that it can make an effective contribution to the situation on Cyprus. When the motion itself is introduced,
Peace Keeping Force to Cyprus we will have an opportunity to explain our views more fully. In the meantime, I can assure the Prime Minister that we will expedite in any way which is necessary the discussion of a motion dealing with this matter.

subsubtopic: PROCEDURE TO ESTABLISH PEACE KEEPING FORCE
speechtext:
I am
sure, Mr. Speaker, that we all regret the situation that has developed on Cyprus that is the occasion of this announcement this afternoon. It is doubly unfortunate in the fact that two members of an alliance designed for mutual protection should now find themselves in a position where they have to be defended from one another. I am sure that we regret this is the situation that has developed, which calls for military intervention in a sense, because we would all much prefer to see the problems settled around the conference table. I think a solution can be found. In view of the fact this proposal has to do with a peace keeping operation, I think it points up once again Canada's willingness to make those sacrifices that are necessary for the preservation of peace.
The urgency of the matter is emphasized by the fact that the local situation could escalate into a world problem and perhaps into a conflagration that would be far reaching in its effects. Certainly, the reports that have appeared in the newspapers are far from reassuring. Perhaps some attention could be given to the possibility, while these nations are asking for assistance, that some activities are being permitted to aggravate the problem and which are directed toward political advantage.
We just want to say this at this time, Mr. Speaker, that we are willing and prepared to co-operate in every possible way to take care of any motion the Prime Minister introduces in connection with this matter. If it requires sitting tonight or tomorrow morning, then we are, in the Social Credit party, prepared to assist and facilitate the consideration of this matter.

subsubtopic: PROCEDURE TO ESTABLISH PEACE KEEPING FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question raised by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) concerning Cyprus is of the utmost importance. We appreciate and understand how serious and far reaching it is. However, what we deplore is that, not only on this occasion but for a good number of years, each time external problems come up, the government, no matter which, Liberal or Conservative, has always shown more interest than it ever did for the problems of our country.
In fact, we have yet to see a government or a prime minister put forward a motion for

Peace Keeping Force to Cyprus an emergency sitting in order to settle the unemployment problem, tor instance, or that of poverty in Canada.
Yet, when Greeks and Turks are fighting each other, we are asked to do so. Since those two countries are members ot NATO,
I feel that the Cyprus problem could have been settled naturally and normally by NATO, without the intervention of any military force. It is due to a lack of good will somewhere that the government is bringing before us a resolution on the advisability of sending troops or not.
I am entirely against the Canadian parliament being asked to sit this evening or tomorrow, or to hold a special sitting in order to consider whether troops should be sent to Cyprus or to that continent. It is not that I am against peace, but I do not believe in peace imposed by arms or under compulsion. I believe in peace brought about through co-operation and agreement. Yes, indeed. For all these reasons, when any government whatsoever gives priority to the problems facing us here in Canada, then I might be more inclined to help it send troops overseas.

If the house will allow me, I should like to ask the Prime Minister one question. Mention was made of the fact that we might sit tonight, if required to do so, or tomorrow. The fact that there has been opposition to sitting tonight or on Saturday denies that unanimity that I hoped would be displayed in this house on a matter that is as important as this one.
However, the question occurs to me, is it necessary that the resolution or motion the Prime Minister will introduce should be considered and passed in the other place? If it is, what arrangements have been made to ensure that the other place is available to consider any resolution that we might pass?

subsubtopic: PROCEDURE TO ESTABLISH PEACE KEEPING FORCE

The right hon. gentleman is, of course, correct. Unanimous consent not being given, we could not meet this evening or tomorrow to deal with this peace keeping situation. The government leader in the Senate was informed that I was to make a statement in the house and he has taken steps to acquaint other leaders in the Senate. He is to make a statement and a resolution will be put forward there at the same time. I do not think we can do anything more at the moment because if we ask permission to interrupt the normal business, that would have to receive unanimous consent, too. Furthermore, we have not yet received final word from New York that the force is legally in being and we cannot pass a resolution authorizing participation in such a force

until we have received that word. In the circumstances I am afraid that is all we can do in this matter at the moment.
I may say I am grateful for the co-operation of the right hon. gentleman the Leader of the Opposition. I am advised by my hon. friend the Secretary of State for External Affairs that in the meantime the Department of National Defence is taking all the necessary preparatory steps so that if parliament does approve a resolution of this kind on Monday we can move forwai'd at once.

Mr. Chairman, it is about a matter related to the administration of the Immigration Act. I wonder if the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Tremblay) can answer the question I put to him a few days ago about the possibility of Algerian farmers settling in Canada, particularly in the province of Quebec?
I am asking that question because it is of interest to the whole country.
In the province of Quebec, and more particularly in my riding of Pontiac-Temis-camingue, a great number of farmers wrote and assured me that in case Algerian colonists would want to settle in Canada, land might be made available to them. Apart from farms occupied at this time, there are a great many abandoned ones both in Pontiac and in Temiscamingue counties. This land was formerly part of prosperous farms.
I have no doubt that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Tremblay) will seriously examine the possibility of establishing those settlers on this land. If he is able to answer the question, would he do so immediately?

Mr. Chairman, some weeks ago, French government officials came to Canada in order to contact authorities in the various departments and provinces in this country, in order to help settle in Canada, a number of Algerian families who are now in France.
Those two officials were quite satisfied with their investigation. They returned to Paris because their report had to be laid before

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration the French government. We helped them as much as possible in their investigation. As far as I know, we have not yet received from the French authorities indications concerning the places the French government might choose for the establishment of those French families.
Several provinces have informed the federal authorities that they would be ready to further the establishment of those French families by paying their expenses and helping them find farm lands.
The department sent a special representative to Paris in order to give the French government all the assistance they might need to reach a decision. Of course, this offer implies a substantial assistance the French government would be prepared to give those immigrants wishing to set up in Canada.
Therefore, we follow closely the developments in that case, and as soon as we have more precise indications concerning the establishment of those French families, it will give me pleasure to pass that information to the hon. member.
Could the minister tell the committee whether he has received representations from the government of the province of Quebec on that matter?

No, Mr. Chairman, the government of the province of Quebec has not indicated its intention to co-operate, but I know that the officials of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration are constantly consulting those of the Quebec department of agriculture on this matter and up to now, this department has greatly co-operated with us with regard to the settlement of these families.

Mr. Chairman, I fully realize that the minister has not held his portfolio very long, and I recognize that it takes a while to get to know all the intricacies and implications of this department. However, I would appreciate it very much if the minister would now make it clear that he is not going to permit anything that might in any way be interpreted as lawyer racketeering in the handling of immigration cases. I have the honour of representing a riding which I think has more of an ethnic basis than any other constituency in western Canada. The result is that I handle a great many immigration cases. I was most disturbed very recently by what I was told in the handling of a case which was drawn to my attention almost a year ago by one of my constituents. This was a case I had taken up with the minister's department, the minister and his predecessor, and I very much appreciate the co-operation

and advice that I received from both ministers. The most recent advice I received from the minister's department was that this particular man should return with his problem to the immigration office and honestly admit that years ago he gave false information; he should give the true information and the entire case would be reconsidered. When I went to the regional office I received the greatest courtesy and co-operation from them, but I was amazed to be told that because a year or two ago chis Chinese person had employed a lawyer to assist him-although I had been handling the case for months- my constituent would have to go through that lawyer. This should not be necessary when a member of parliament is handling a case and has received co-operation and advice from the minister's department, and I may say that I received the advice of the minister himself. I fail to understand why, in these circumstances, a member of parliament should be told by a regional office, when he goes there in accordance with the instructions of the minister or his department, that his constituent must pay a lawyer to handle his case.
I think this is a mistake. I wish to say that I understand it was not under your direction, sir, but some time ago such an instruction was issued. There must have been some such instruction issued, otherwise I as a member of parliament would not have been told that in recent weeks when I took up this case in Vancouver. I believe there is something radically wrong when an East Indian, a Chinese person or anybody else who is having his case handled by his member of parliament is told this. Although we may receive every courtesy and co-operation, it seems that we must advise our constituents to have their cases handled through the lawyer in order that it may be proceeded with further. That is what I meant when I said I hope the minister will make an early acceptance of his responsibility, and make it clear that a problem case which is being handled by a member of the House of Commons does not have to go through a lawyer, because I know what they charge my constituents to handle their immigration problems. Furthermore, judging from his previous remarks, we are of the opinion that the present Minister of Citizenship and Immigration is no longer qualified to head that department, and that is exactly the point we wish to underscore. Furthermore, I maintain that his statement is contrary to the opinion held by those favouring the implementation of an immigration policy in Canada at the present time.

Mr. Chairman, I want to direct a few remarks to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, identical to those I directed to the former minister. I do so because this is the first opportunity I have had of speaking since the minister assumed this portfolio, and I am hoping he will bring as high a degree of enthusiasm to the workings of the Indian affairs branch as did his predecessor.
I realize it is not an easy matter for a minister overnight to change procedures that have been going on for decades. Nevertheless, there is something he could do, if he were prepared to take a single administrative decision and see to it that his officials carried it out, a decision that would result in immediate and future benefits for all Indian people.
I ask that the minister deal with the director of the Indian affairs branch and the chief of the welfare division of that branch, to see to it that rates of financial assistance to Indians are standardized with those rates of assistance being offered by other social agencies across Canada in the communities in which Indians are living.

There is no excuse for there being such a great disparity between the amount of assistance a person who is a registered Indian can receive in comparison with the amount a non-Indian in identical circumstances can receive. It is more than just a matter of seeing to it that an Indian person in need has sufficient resources available to him to preserve health and decency. There is something more important at stake.
We are faced with the problem of walls being built between one group of Canadian citizens and another. The question of unity and harmony between various races is one, I am sure, that occupies the minds of the government, as it occupies the minds of all thinking Canadians. Nothing divides people quite as effectively or harmfully as when the rate or form of help they are able to get is completely dependant on whether their parents were Indians or not, which is what the present system is, in effect.
This means that an Indian person in a given community cannot get help from an agency from which others are getting help. It means he must go to an Indian agent. Furthermore, it means that when that person at last establishes his need for assistance, be it financial or otherwise, in every case the level of assistance is not as adequate as that which would be available to someone else, someone who might be a Greek or a Frenchman, or in the case of the Northwest Territories, an Eskimo or a white.
The solution to this problem rests in an administrative decision to be made by the minister in consultation with his welfare officials. I am sure no hon. member would begrudge the additional dollars it might cost if the minister, when presenting his next estimates, is able to say that Indian people who find themselves in need of assistance will, in every case, receive the same level of assistance as would a non-Indian in similar circumstances.
1 note in the supplementary estimates an item for the granting of $25,000 to the province of Manitoba to assist in its work in community development with people of Indian origin. The prospects that community development programs hold for Indian people are very great. The minister may not have been in his department long enough to familiarize himself fully with the community development program being carried out in Manitoba, or with the one that is starting in Saskatchewan, but there is no doubt, on the basis of preliminary studies, that the dollar invested in a community development kind of program pays off, not only in reduced social welfare and human costs but in accelerating the pace at which Indian people are

I would ask the minister to consider convening a conference on community development with the various community development services in existence across Canada, in the light of the experience which community development organizations in the United States have, such a conference to consider the role that a healthy and sound community development program can play in assisting the Indian people to integrate themselves more speedily than has been the case in the past.
I am sure all hon. members welcome the announcement which the minister made yesterday, in response to questions, that legislation on the Indian claims commission will be introduced later this session, and that there is no intention on the part of the government to let the matter lapse, or drop it entirely.
I am hopeful that the minister will not insist that the letters which were sent out to every Indian band in Canada-I believe there was almost 1,000 letters-must be replied to before the resolution preceding the legislation can be introduced. While it is important that the Indian bands should have been notified of what the government was proposing to do, surely we cannot afford to wait until every Indian band has replied?
For one thing, many Indian people are unaccustomed to being consulted by any government with regard to what is going to happen to them, and quite frankly many of them do not know what this correspondence is all about. I made a recent trip through the Northwest Territories, and I saw the documents that the former minister sent to the Indian people pinned to walls, alongside my picture and the pictures of all other important officials, in their eyes.
Many of them really did not understand the document because it was written in excellent civil serviceese. They did not understand what is being asked of them, and consequently I suspect that it is being treated as another piece of paper that is interesting, but which does not really hold out any hope of improvement for them. So I would ask the minister to set a target date, and if necessary write to his field officials and ask them to get this information back as quickly as possible. If it is not available within two or three weeks I would ask the minister not to sit back and say that they cannot establish this Indian claims commission because they have not heard from the people on the Thunderchild reserve, or some other place like that.
