The Indian claims commission holds tremendous promise for the Indian people of Canada. They are very keen on it. I have referred before to the efforts the previous minister made in dealing with the Indian people to assure them that the government was going to proceed with this commission. I assure the present minister, as I did the past, that the Indian people are keen on the commission. Do not betray their trust and do not, through inaction, allow their enthusiasm to wane and permit this commission to go the way of so many other projects.
If the minister has been following the press closely in relation to Indian matters he will have noted in recent weeks the fact that an Indian from the Northwest Territories, Michael Sikkyea, was convicted some months ago of the unpardonable offence of killing a duck in the spring and his guns, equipment and so on were seized. The case was reviewed by the next higher court of the Northwest Territories and a decision was given quashing the earlier conviction. Subsequently the case was referred to the appeal court of the Northwest Territories, which ruled that the provisions of the Migratory Birds Convention Act applied to Michael Sikkyea, and his conviction was confirmed. Because the decision was unanimous it is now necessary for Michael Sikkyea to seek the permission of the Supreme Court of Canada to appeal.
An Edmonton lawyer has taken it upon himself to assist Mr. Sikkyea in bringing this matter before the Supreme Court of Canada, but because this is an important problem for all Indian people I want to make a suggestion at this time. The minister can take notice of it and perhaps let me or the house know his answer. Does the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, Indian affairs branch, have any way in which it can assist Indian people with legal expenses when they become involved in these areas that are still very much in doubt? Surely it is the function of the branch responsible for helping the Indian people to have within the branch some kind of contingency fund so that Indian people, who through no fault of their own or through a misunderstanding of the law become involved in offences and may not have access to expert legal advice, will be provided with this assistance. I ask the minister merely to take this question as notice. I have mentioned these various matters because I know that as a new minister he has not had time to look into all of them, but by bringing them to his attention perhaps he will take them up with his officials.
I should like him to give the house the assurance that he will have the courage to look into the matter of the level of financial

assistance to Indian people, discuss it with his officers and, if necessary, make the courageous, administrative decision that the Indian people shall no longer receive less financial assistance when they are in need than other people in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, may I add something on that very point? I believe I am correct that the province of British Columbia is going to appeal the decision further. This Indian has no money. When he appealed, his position was found to be correct and the original conviction was quashed. Surely in a matter of this importance there is a responsibility on the minister's department to assist this Indian financially. I just wanted to mention this case in support of the statement made by the previous speaker and to ask the department to give very serious consideration to legal assistance to Indians and Eskimos under similar circumstances.

The purposes of this bill, as set out in the explanatory notes, is to deal with a situation which came to my mind a couple of years ago when the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) had an argument with the Minister of Veterans Affairs over the appointment or the reappointment of people serving on public boards.

speechtext:
Just last spring-an interjection has come from the hon. member concerned.
It struck me at the time that there was a real hardship involved on occasion in these appointments to boards, councils and so on, in respect of which there is a definite time period. In case after case, when a person is well under the normal age of retirement and might reasonably expect his appointment to be renewed, he finds himself removed from his position right at the last minute, due to an exercise of ministerial discretion. It seems to me it would be only fair in such cases to allow for six months' notice to be given. I think this would have the effect not only of protecting the persons involved but also of allowing the ministries concerned to make a more careful appraisal of the performance of persons who hold such offices.
The one part of this bill which, I say myself, may contain a weakness, has to do with the situation which would arise should a change in the government of the day coincide with the termination of a great number of appointments of the kind which are the subject of this measure. This would mean, I suppose a delay of about six months before the new government could hand out these positions to its own followers, as seems to be largely the case. However, I do not think this would impose a tremendous burden.
The other point I should like to make is this: I believe we are moving away from patronage. I think it is being recognized that the calibre of the people who are required to serve on many of these boards-the pensions board is an example-is such that the partisan label placed on those who fill these offices, or the assumption that they are no more than party followers being rewarded for good party work, is becoming less and less popular in the country.
For this reason I think the bill would do a great deal of good. I know some hon. members may say that anyone who takes on such an appointment is aware that at the end of his appointment it may not be renewed. But I think when an appointment lasts five, six or seven years there is a tendency for it to develop into a routine. If you want to look at this matter historically, there is no question that if you want to find fault you can find it with Conservatives or with Liberals.
Criminal Code
I know that some people who were appointed by the Liberal government during the 22 years they were in office suddenly, at the end of their term of office, while they still had many good years of work ahead of them and were well below what we might think of as being the normal retirement age, did not have their appointments renewed. I know this did not happen in connection with the board in which my hon. friend was interested-at least, I do not believe it did- but I believe it did happen with the tariff board.
The protection afforded by this bill would not affect a great many people; yet it seems to me it is something worth having, in all fairness. I have been interested more in the board of broadcast governors, perhaps, than in any of the other boards of government. At the present time we have three full time members of that board who I conceive would be affected by this bill. I know that in a couple of years time the question will arise with regard to their reappointments. You have on the board-I shall deal with personalities-Dr. Stewart and Mr. Carlyle Allison. It seems to me there is a great likelihood that in either case, but particularly in the case of Mr. Allison, the government at the time, if it should happen to be other than a Conservative government, may feel they do not want to renew Mr. Allison's appointment. I would agree they are entitled not to renew it, but I believe that in view of the long period of service given by Mr. Allison, despite the fact that in the past he may have been considered a Conservative partisan representative before he took on this position, he would have the entitlement of six months notice. Of course this notice could be served six months before the appointment lapsed; the only requirement would be six months.
I do not think this is a major item. It would just redress, it seems to me, a situation in which harm could be done to Canadians who enter government service. I think it is one of the small things we can do to improve the attractions of government posts. I have heard from cabinet ministers in both the Conservative government and the present government that it is terribly difficult to get many Canadians to serve on boards. Quite often the argument is put forward that a change of government will come along and they will find it very difficult. One of the explanations often given to me as the reason so many appointees are partisan appointees is that non-partisan appointees tend to turn down these appointments because of the lack of security, and the fact that they may be labelled and may not have any protection. It seems to me this small amendment would help solve this problem.

Criminal Code
Mr. Speaker, as I close these rather brief introductory remarks I should like to say a word to those who may wonder about "a purge for the king's evil". The king's evil is thought of in two ways. In medical terms the king's evil is a type of scrofula that is no longer as prevalent as it used to be, probably because of modern sanitary methods. The other reference to it is the arbitrary use of power. In this sense the bill would prevent the arbitrary intervention or use of ministerial power in cases where an appointment to one of the government boards or agencies is lapsing, without giving this notice. This bill, as the explanatory notes say, "preserves the crown's right to dismiss without notice but protects the interest of the employee and the public interest". The reason for the Criminal Code being introduced here is, of course, that it would be tremendously difficult to go through and rewrite or amend every statute which creates the membership for boards. By making this a penalty that would apply to a minister, in particular, who was involved in such a case there is produced, it seems to me, the required effect. Of course, I am sure that once the amendment was made it would just become part of the understanding around the federal civil service, and in a sense would be merely a signboard.
I hope the house will consider the matter fairly. I have not tried to go into a great deal of detail about the pros and cons of charges that have been made through our history regarding the arbitrary dismissal of people, because I did not think that was worth while. I hope all hon. members will join with me in supporting this bill.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to respond to the remarks of our distinguished hon. friend with respect to his Bill No. C-ll. speechtext:
There is a great advantage in the objectivity of the ivory tower approach, or being able to look at something in theory or principle. However, sometimes the fact that one looks at government in this theoretic

way deprives that person of some of the considerations that are very important in a truly objective analysis.
The hon. member referred to an appointment to which I will not allude specifically, although I think the case he had in mind could very well be argued on its merits. The former minister of veterans affairs appointed to the pension board a person whom he had come to know, trust and respect; and subsequently, when the period of his service had expired, this appointment was not renewed. Another minister, looking at his responsibilities with a fresh point of view, approached the problem with a view to re-establishing a balance which he believed to be of value. I suggest that each of these gentlemen did his job, in the making of these appointments, honestly and fairly.
What does this disgusting word "patronage" really means? If we go back far enough, patronage was where an ecclesiastical power, such as a bishop or somebody like that, took a monk who was scrubbing the floors, serving at table and serving the candles and, because he had certain gifts, turned him to the translation of the scriptures or allowed him to paint on the walls or develop the arts. Patronage, in the finest sense, is the power of the ministry to take talent and to put it to work. After all, one of the main considerations when a government changes is actually to change the direction of government in the way the new set of politicians believe it should be shifted and changed. Indeed if we do not take the attitude that there can be change, there is very little merit in elections at all. I am not arguing that my party has all the political wisdom because I do not think it has. But we have had a change of government which resulted from the defeat of the former government on February 5, 1963.
Looking at this bill in the context of what happened since February 5, 1963 there were, according to my count-I am referring now to sessional paper No. 249

99 orders in council passed by the government that had been defeated. They made appointments to the Senate, to lieutenant governorships, judges, returning officers, the Atlantic development board, Canada Council, ambassadors, the consular service, Canadian Overseas Telecommunications Corporation, agricultural products board, national film board, Farm Credit Corporation, Canadian Pension Commission, national battlefields commission, national productivity council, Canadian Commercial Corporation, national technical and vocational training and advisory council, defence research board, national research council and the tariff board. They appointed directors of the Bank of Canada, board referees under the

Unemployment Insurance Act, and so on. These included some of the most critical appointments involving well over 200 key people employed in the public service of Canada.
I am not criticizing this, Mr. Speaker, but I am pointing out the danger in adding this inflexibility which is inherent in this particular bill. Because surely one of the things which a new administration has to do, if it can, is in its own wisdom to shift direction. I am not arguing now that these appointments which were made were not good appointments, that they were not honestly conceived to be in the best interests of Canada by the former administration. But they would not be the appointments of a successive government, and what is the use of an election if a successive government cannot in some wise change the direction of policy.
By way of contrast I should like to indicate the type of people who surrounded the rather interesting democratic administration of the late John Kennedy. A lot of books have been written on this subject. I could refer hon. members to a book called: "The New Frontiersmen" published by Public Affairs Press, "The Year of Trial", "The Study of the Kennedy Circle", etc. It was my privilege, as a member of our defence committee under the chairmanship of the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Sauve), to be in Washington on December 11, 1963. There we had a chance to sit in and talk to William Bundy, assistant secretary of defence, J. C. Kitchen, Mr. Henry S. Rowen, Mr. D. Gilchrist, and other gentlemen. Afterwards I had a chance at leisure to talk to some of these people. And what was the phenomenon which took place? Within a few months a new administration was able to make new appointments unfettered by the kind of law that my distinguished friend from Port Arthur-

Hon. members will recall that, owing to the untimely death of John Kennedy his vice president took over the office of president. That meant that there was absolutely no security of tenure of the officials of the United States administration. As a matter of fact our defence committee had hoped earlier that there would be an opportunity for a talk with Mr. Robert McNamara, but circumstances at that time were such that nobody quite knew just what confidence Mr. McNamara might enjoy in the new administration. With respect, Mr. Speaker, any shift in direction on the part of a new administration which is at all creative depends in some measure on the quality and prestige of the type of people who enter the service of the government. This bill affords a certain added protection in time to all existing appointees. If the bill has merit why not extend the time to a year, a year and a half or two years? It is perfectly clear from the fact that some security of continued employment is now provided that for some time any new administration has to gradually work its way through to effect the changes which it thinks are in the national interest. Unless this country can take some leaves out of the books of other democratic states such as West Germany, some of the Scandinavian countries and Britain, what we are going to do is to limp along in an archaic, Victorian way, unappropriate to these difficult and rather demanding times. The American experience is something which we might well look at.
Because the fact is today every government is tested to some extent by the quality of just such appointments. The word patronage covers the very best appointments and the very poorest. We know, on a general principle of course, the large bulk of our public servants are going to be employed by the choice of the civil service commission, unfettered in their wisdom, but there is a certain residue, a certain area, where the ministry does have some choice, and this Bill C-ll is obviously a step which tends to limit and reduce that choice of movement.
As it happens, and I feel the matter is relevant, the Kennedy administration is about as good an example as we might find of an administrative body seeking out the talent of people either in the universities, in private business, in journalism or the professions, and it is those kind of people we want to help share the risks which politicians know, to try to do something for their country.
Everyone in this house, from the Prime Minister to the newest member of the house-

That is a good thing for the house, for us and for Canada, and there are some people who never wish to risk getting into practical politics themselves, but they are willing to come along with us and share the risks. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, a good many of these appointments have been covered by orders in council of the former administration-99 of them.
What possible benefit does it do to penalize the minister? One of the principles of criminal law is that if a man commits a crime there has to be some evidence of mens rea, or guilty mind, but my hon. friend who has introduced this bill has not introduced that element at all. If a minister should fail to fire a man at the proper time, six months before his time expires then he automatically becomes eligible for an additional six months. That is not good principle or law.
There are people in this country from the best areas of agriculture, of labour movements, of the universities and industry who are prepared to step in with politicians and take a chance to do something for the national interest. I am satisfied that if we further limit the choice of the government by adding security, simply shoring up any job, any appointment, then what we are doing is simply reducing that flexibility and that change.
I can quite understand that occasionally there are people who are hurt, and who perhaps should not be hurt. I think that is one of the misfortunes of the democratic process; but surely it is much more important to Canada that there be some flexibility, some change in direction?
I have heard the distinguished hon. member who introduced this bill stand up and say there is no difference between the Liberal party and the Conservative party when they are in power.

But let us face another fact, that generally those who run for office and win seats in this House of Commons are pretty average types, but some of them possess the ability to pick out better brains than their own. We have to be on the lookout all the time for imaginative, adventurous, daring people who are prepared-not necessarily in practical politics but rather in the area of service to Her Majesty in the public service-to take the risks involved and help mould and direct new events.
I did not intend to speak at length, Mr. Speaker, but I know something of the circumstances of the case that prompted this bill. Mr. Speaker, I would first like to express my profound regret at the speech I have just listened to from the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson). A week or so ago I had occasion to congratulate him on a speech he made in the house, but I now regret I did because he has destroyed my confidence in him by the speech he has delivered this afternoon.
He is inferring that the government exists only if it pursues the course of patronage and surrounds itself with people of the same mind and intent, and that when a government changes, then there should be a very substantial change in the civil service. This is disturbing. I thought that for the past 40 years we had settled the limitation on patronage within the ranks of the civil service, but the hon. member for Leeds wants to revive it.
Perhaps this accounts for the bill now before us and for the complaint I made earlier with regard to an example of Liberal action concerning a person in the public service.
Criminal Code
I see no relationship whatsoever with the situation in the United States where, when there is a change in government, about 5,000 people employed by the government leave and are supplanted by 5,000 others of a different political philosophy. That is a different system from what is supported here, except to a very limited extent, for example where personal assistants to a prime minister and other ministers do not stay on to advise a succeeding prime minister. But within the civil service, and within our various boards and commissions, we have provided for security of tenure and continuity.
The hon. member for Leeds in mentioning a particular case, which is the one that apparently inspired the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) to bring forward this bill, and which encourages me to speak on it, mentioned the fact that this particular person was closely associated with me in a political sense, and as though this were terribly wrong.

I do not want to misinterpret the hon. gentleman but I would point out to him, and this has been mentioned before by the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Teillet), that he is talking about people associated with me in political activity and then drawn into public service. Why did he not give the example of the vice chairman of the pension commission, who sat here as a member of the House of Commons and resigned his seat to take the appointment of vice chairman of that commission? That was a political appointment if there ever was one. He remained on the pension commission and we did not remove him.
I support the bill advanced by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) in principle. I do not agree with the penalty clauses he has provided, but the introductory paragraph in the explanatory notes outlines the purpose of the bill and this has my support. It reads as follows:
The purpose of this bill is to ensure that public servants who are appointed for a period of time to boards, commissions and other public offices in the gift of the crown shall be given six months' notice if they are not to be reappointed. Thus the dismissee has time to prepare for his transition from employment to unemployment.

Criminal Code
Surely that is only fair. I would never agree to any other action being taken with regard to people employed on boards or commissions if they desire a little time to make the adjustment to some new job. Nobody is talking about keeping them on for a year and a half or two years or anything like that. The purpose is to provide a six month period for adjustment.
Just about a year ago this coming May I raised an objection about the scandalous action, as I considered it, of the Liberal Government in removing from office on four days notice or less a member of the pension commission. I wondered why they were so foolish. Why did they not give Mr. Ken McKay three months' notice or six months' notice if they did not want to continue him in office? To dismiss him practically overnight was in my opinion shocking-and particularly to start doing such things with the pension commission, of all boards or commissions in this country, a commission which has been free from political interference. Despite political appointments to that commission it has been free from political interference. It represents the veterans of this country. The members of the commission are themselves veterans.
The first act of the present Minister of Veterans Affairs was to retire from office a veteran of the first world war, without any reason given at all except that the minister said that his time was up. Over the years the practice on the pension commission has been to appoint people generally to what are called ad hoc positions and such positions are renewable from year to year. When vacancies occur on the permanent staff of the commission the ad hoc commissioners are normally advanced to those permanent positions.
Mr. Ken McKay was an ad hoc appointment on a one year basis and his reappointment came up last May. The normal practice observed by other ministers of veterans affairs has been to continue these ad hoc appointments. My predecessor in office, the hon. Mr. Brooks, carried out that practice and I did, myself. An appointee of the former Liberal government was continued as an ad hoc commissioner for 17 years. Year after year renewal of his appointment took place.
The particular member of the pension commission to whom I have referred was retired practically overnight. I objected to that very strenuously and protested the action in a telegram which I sent to the Minister of Veterans Affairs on May 2 and which he answered by letter. I apprised the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) of the situation and he did not bother to reply to the cable I sent
[Mr. Churchill.)
to him in London. I sent him another telegram when he came back to Canada and at that point he replied in these words:
I do not believe this is a matter in which I should interfere with the decision of the responsible minister.
He washed his hands of a matter affecting a veteran of this country. He washed his hands of a matter affecting the pension commission which should be kept free of political interference. It was to this attitude that I objected, this striking at the veterans of this country through the pension commission immediately on the Liberal government taking office. It was almost the first act of the Liberal government last year. This veteran had served in the first world war and, as I pointed out in my telegram, had been through the battle of Passchendale.

speechtext:
I would not have Ventured to ask for the leave of the house to bring forward this motion had I not been convinced by information I have received that there has been a very serious deterioration in the situation on the island of Cyprus, which constitutes a real threat to peace and security in that area. And if there is a threat to peace and security in any area of the world today there is a threat to peace and security in every area of the world.
I indicated earlier in the day that if certain developments took place at the United

Peace Keeping Force to Cyprus Nations in New York, it would be possible, provided the house so agreed, to consider this matter in the light of those developments.
I would like, in the first place, to report to the house and put on the record a statement made by the secretary general of the United Nations at a meeting of the security council late this afternoon. The secretary general made this statement:
It may be recalled that in my report to the council of yesterday, March 12, I expressed my confidence that the United Nations peace keeping force in Cyprus would be soon established, and indicated that I hoped shortly to be able to report some positive developments. It is with considerable gratification that I am able to inform the council that the force now is actually being constituted.
Since late yesterday, I have received firm and official assurances from three of the governments I have approached about providing contingents that those contingents will be available. These governments are: Canada, Ireland and Sweden. With regard to each of these governments, certain conditions and prerequisites were defined, which either have been met or, in my view, can be coped with.
The secretary general then goes on:
I may add that there are other promising prospects for troops. In these circumstances, therefore, I am now able to state to the council that the force will be established without further delay, and that elements of it will soon be deployed in Cyprus. Indeed, a small party of Canadian officers will be en route to Cyprus tonight.
That is the part I mentioned to the house this afternoon. The secretary general went on:
This morning I received a communication through the permanent representative of Turkey to the United Nations which has since been issued as a security council document. I immediately requested the permanent representative to convey to his government my serious concern and my urgent appeal to exercise the utmost restraint. A formal reply to this communication has also been sent.
The council is also aware of the pledges of voluntary financial contributions which I have already received from several governments, which assure the requisite financial support for the United Nations peace keeping force in Cyprus. I am most grateful to all these governments for their ready and generous response.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the statement issued only an hour or so ago by the secretary general and which I think indicates that a United Nations peace keeping force has now been constituted. I think we will all agree that the sooner that force can get to Cyprus, where the situation is deteriorating, the better it will be for peace and security. It is our purpose to ask this house to approve of a contribution by Canada to this force for this high and noble purpose.
Mr. Speaker, although the house has been in a general way kept informed of developments in so far as it was possible to do that while those developments were proceeding and changing so rapidly-that is, developments in the island of Cyprus-perhaps it would be

helpful if I reviewed briefly some of the major factors in the situation which have led the government to submit this resolution seeking approval for Canadian participation in a United Nations peace keeping force for Cyprus. Events move very rapidly these days, and it is hard to realize now that it was only on March 4 that the secretary general of the United Nations made an official request to the Canadian government to contribute a contingent to this force. This request came as a result of a security council resolution passed that same day which recommended the creation of a force and the appointment of a mediator. The security council in that resolution recommended that the function of the force should be, and I quote from the resolution:
-in the interest of preserving international peace and security to use its best efforts to prevent a recurrence of fighting and, as necessary, to contribute to the maintenance and restoration of law and order and a return to normal conditions.
It further recommended that the stationing of the force should be for a period of three months only. This means, Mr. Speaker, that if the force is required in Cyprus for a longer period than three months-and I do not believe we should have any illusions about the necessity of this-that could only be done if the security council passes another resolution. The prospect of Canada being approached had been foreseen by the government from the outset. I think we in Canada can take some pride in the fact that whenever the United Nations is required to intervene in a situation where peace and security are threatened, the United Nations has nearly always turned to Canada for assistance. Canada has always been proud to do its full duty in this respect.

subsubtopic: KEEPING FORCE

subsubtopic: KEEPING FORCE
speechtext: This is a matter, I think, of pride for us all. But it also involves problems and difficulties. My right hon. friend, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker) was the head of a government which was faced with this problem when a serious situation arose in the Congo and Canada, under his leadership, at that time responded quickly and effectively.

subsubtopic: KEEPING FORCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: KEEPING FORCE
speechtext: Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, it is not inappropriate for me to recall tonight that in those days one of the strongest and most sincere supporters of the United Nations action in this field was the man who was secretary of state for external affairs in those-days, Mr. Howard Green.

subsubtopic: KEEPING FORCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: KEEPING FORCE
speechtext:
I think all of us are deeply concerned about the inherent danger of sharp conflict developing out of this Cyprus situation between two neighbouring countries who are, with Canada, members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. I refer to Greece and Turkey. In addition to doing anything we can as a member of the United Nations to prevent a conflict between two members of the Atlantic coalition, we also wish to play our part in rendering whatever assistance we can to restore peace and order to Cyprus, which is a fellow member of the commonwealth of nations. There is every humanitarian reason, Mr. Speaker, for doing what we can to halt violence and bloodshed on that beautiful and once happy island. We in Canada have always regarded participation in United Nations peace keeping operations as a fundamental obligation of United Nations membership, as our service in Korea, the Congo, the Middle East, Kashmir and Indochina, testifies. So on March 6 our permanent representative to the United Nations, on instructions, indicated our interest as a government in playing our full part in this operation. But he also, on instructions from the government, raised certain questions with the secretary general with a view to ascertaining what were the facts of the situation in Cyprus and what would be the nature of the peace keeping operations. We wanted to ensure that if we took part in this operation we would at least get whatever assurance could be secured that we would have an opportunity to discharge that duty.
Therefore the permanent representative asked the secretary general certain questions, and these followed the lines of the statement which I made in the house on February 19. In that statement I laid down what I thought were reasonable conditions which should attach to our participation and, indeed, to the participation of other members in this United Nations operation. Among the important questions which were put to the secretary general at that time were those relating to the size and composition of the force and the role envisaged for the forces in Cyprus.
The right hon. gentleman said this afternoon, the United Nations would be intervening in a situation of civil war. Civil war is always tragic, but is even more tragic and dangerous to general peace and security when the two parties to the civil war are backed by outside states, as is the case in Cyprus. Therefore we wanted information on that point. We wanted to be quite certain that the powers and authority which were to be allocated to the United Nations force would be sufficient to ensure that it be given the chance to do the job it w7as sent to do. We wanted to be sure that the force would have
Peace Keeping Force to Cyprus enough authority under its terms of reference to give itself protection, because we also had a responsibility in that regard. We were particularly concerned with these matters, and I am sure no hon. member would wish me to apologize for this concern which we have shown. Because we knew that this United Nations force would be asked to perform perhaps a more difficult and dangerous role than that entrusted to any United Nations operation since the formation of the world organization.
One prerequisite which we laid down for Canadian participation was that the force should be multinational in character. We have now received from the secretary general, as I indicated a few moments ago, word which satisfies this requirement. In addition to Canada there will be other contingents participating in the force. There will be a Swedish contingent, an Irish contingent, and we also hope, though the secretary general did not mention it in his statement to the security council, that a Finnish contingent will be sent, along with the British, Turkish and Greek contingents which are now on the island and will participate as representatives of the guarantor powers in the situation there.
I am sure I do not need to tell this house how complex and dangerous is the situation in Cyprus. There is a very obvious danger to peace because intercommunal strife in the island is closely related, as I have pointed out, to the interests of Greece and Turkey which have treaty rights that permit them to intervene in the island in certain circumstances. While that is true, the problem is basically intercommunal, arising out of a dispute over the constitution. Incidentally, it is interesting to recall that the chief justice who has the authority and the problem of interpreting that constitution, is Mr. Justice Wilson, a member of the Ontario supreme court.
I suggest that this problem can be solved only in a climate of moderation and compromise, removed from violence and bloodshed. The need for a mediator to bring that about has been recognized, even though that mediator has not been appointed. But if the mediator is going to do his job, there has to be peace on the island. It will be the purpose of the international force to bring about, if it can, a situation of sufficient peace to enable a mediator to go to work and bring about a political settlement which will remove, to the greatest extent possible, the chances of this kind of bloodshed and disturbance in the future.
I am sorry that there has been a delay in the appointment of a mediator. I think back

Peace Keeping Force to Cyprus to the tragic days of 1956 when the United Nations intervened in Palestine to keep the peace. If the United Nations had had perhaps two or three days to move in with a mediator, who had been charged with the responsibility of trying to bring out of this crisis, this panic almost, a political settlement, that might have been done. But that opportunity passed, and once the United Nations force moved in-and it is still there many years afterwards-the danger of that conflict spreading was at least halted. Then the atmosphere changed, and it was very hard indeed to bring about a political settlement; and there has been very little improvement in that field ever since. So I would hope that a mediator can move into Cyprus as quickly as possible, take advantage of the present emergency situation, and out of that emergency bring about some kind of political settlement which will avoid this kind of request for action from the United Nations in the future. But that is going to be a very difficult task indeed for any mediator.
The government, and I am sure the house too, have no illusions about the difficulty and danger of the task which will face our forces in Cyprus if the house supports this resolution. Peace keeping operations are very rarely easy. They are usually expensive. They are uncertain in duration and they are very often subject to unfortunate incidents. Who would have thought that when we moved into Palestine in 1956 Canadian contingents in the United Nations emergency force would be still there today, keeping guard on that disturbed frontier?
Therefore the responsibilities which we are asking the house to approve will not be taken lightly, I know, by the house. The force which will be stationed in Cyprus will not act as an army of occupation. It will be a reserve of impartial strength, but its success will depend in large measure on the co-operation of the Greek and Turkish communities in Cyprus and on the support and co-operation of the governments of Greece and Turkey. The United Nations force there, under the blue flag of peace of our world organization may, however, even by its very presence, bring about that easing of the atmosphere which will make some kind of solution possible. And perhaps we should not forget that while the force will consist, so it is now anticipated, of about 7,000 members, half of those will be members of the forces of Her Majesty, Queen of the United Kingdom, who have been holding the line in Cyprus at a time of very great provocation, difficulty and danger. Half of whom will be changing over from membership in the United Kingdom force to temporary membership in the United Nations force,

and will be serving with British and Canadian forces, who have served together so many times. It will be a very happy circumstance indeed, and I would like to think of it as having significance beyond Cyprus, if in this partnership of British and Canadian forces in a peace keeping operation, we can once again associate with the Irish forces.
The Canadian contingent to the peace keeping force will consist of a self-contained battalion group augmented by a reconnaissance squadron. Administrative and logistic support elements will also be provided. The 2nd battalion of the Royal 22nd regiment now stationed at Valcartier and currently on stand-by duty for United Nations service -and I may say we have kept a battalion on stand-by duty for this kind of service, the 2nd battalion of this famous and courageous regiment, and a reconnaissance squad-dron of the Royal Canadian Dragoons, now in Gagetown, have been selected for this honourable and dangerous duty.
These two fine regiments, which have in the past been responsible for many creditable pages in Canadian history, will go to this new duty with the confidence and trust of the Canadian government and the Canadian people.
The Canadian contribution, if parliament supports a contribution, will be air lifted by R.C.A.F. transport command to Nicosia with their personal arms and equipment, over a period of two weeks or so. A small fact finding force, as I indicated to the house this afternoon, has already left for Cyprus and will be reporting to the United Nations representative there, so that it can at once send back information as to what the arrangements will be and what the requirements will be. Her Majesty's Canadian ship Bonaventure, which returned to Halifax today, may have a role in the transportation of vehicles and material to Cyprus. The Canadian contingent is expected to number approximately 1,050 officers and men, and in addition there will be an R.C.A.F. element of up to 100.
The arrangements for the financing of the United Nations force are a departure from the established practice, and from what is desirable. In that respect I wholeheartedly agree with what the right hon. Leader of the Opposition said this afternoon about the undesirability of this kind of arrangement, that a few members of the United Nations should have to do more than their duty, financial and otherwise, to make up for the dereliction of duty on the part of other members of the United Nations.

subsubtopic: KEEPING FORCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: KEEPING FORCE
speechtext:
A voluntary fund is to be created to which the United States has

pledged $2 million, and the United Kingdom $1 million in addition to its own contribution, and I believe other countries have already contributed to the fund.
The Canadian government, Mr. Speaker, has consistently held-the present government and its predecessors-that the financing of United Nations peace keeping operations should be the collective responsibility of the whole membership, and I do not know how we can continue satisfactorily to carry on those operations unless some arrangements of that kind are made in the United Nations. But in the rapidly deteriorating situation which we face in Cyprus, and which was made so clear to us by the messages we received today and yesterday, it seemed clear that the deployment of a United Nations force could not wait upon lengthy financial negotiations. The government has therefore decided to assume all the costs of a Canadian contingent for a three month period, as well as the costs of transporting our men and our materials to Cyprus. The estimate, and of course it is only an estimate, of the total costs for three months, including a one-way airlift, is about $2,600,000.
I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that this is not the way to carry on a United Nations operation where a few members-and they are becoming increasingly fewer and are becoming concentrated among a certain circle of United Nations members-have to bear not so much the financial responsibility as the political and every other kind of responsibility, in discharging the duties of the United Nations in regard to peace keeping operations.
Perhaps I may be permitted to pay my tribute to the hard work which the Secretary of State for External Affairs has been doing in the last few days in trying, not only to bring about a satisfactory solution of the problem of a Canadian contribution, but to get the force itself into operation. He has been on the telephone today, I think to Turkey, Sweden, Finland, Ireland, New York, and perhaps even to Windsor. I can only say that if his predecessor were around Ottawa these days I think he would have been proud of the activities of the secretary of state.
Yesterday, the Secretary of State for External Affairs said this, and I do not apologize for putting it on the record, because I think it will meet general agreement in the house:
Once again, the urgent requirements in Cyprus have illustrated the need to prepare in advance for prompt United Nations engagement in peace keeping operations. This is a matter of contingent planning in United Nations headquarters by military and political staffs, of earmarking, training and equipping units and personnel in national defence establishments, of improving methods for processing United Nations requests for assistance, of standardizing operational procedures.
Canadian views in this regard have been stated so often-
Peace Keeping Force to Cyprus -by the present government and by its
predecessor-
-that it is hardly necesary for me to do more than mention them. We have been pressing for the establishment of a military planning staff which could assist the secretary general and his political advisers in establishing and conducting peace keeping operations. Canada has been exploring ways and means of making its own stand-by arrangements more effective.
Other member states share our views about earmarking and training troops for United Nations service. The Nordic countries and the Netherlands have firm policies in this regard. Recent indications are that more governments are thinking along the same lines.
Last autumn the Canadian delegation to the assembly suggested that it might be useful to pool experience and ideas for improving United Nations peacemaking methods. Because of prevailing international political circumstances, this cannot be done at the present time through formal action by the United Nations. For the time being, interested members may have to accept that a permanent peace keeping force cannot be established, although it has emerged as one of the ultimate goals of disarmament programs put forward in Geneva.
Yet Cyprus and other situations already on the international horizon show that peace keeping operations by the United Nations may be needed on very short notice. The demands are almost as varied as the situations which arise. In Greece, Kashmir and Palestine, military observers on the ground were needed. In Lebanon and Yemen, air observers played a key role.
In Gaza and the Congo, an international force was essential. On many occasions, the United Nations has urgently needed mediators and conciliators.
The obvious conclusion is that the United Nations cannot stand still in its preparations for such operations. It has accumulated experience but some of the lessons have been learned the hard way. The underlying risk of escalation to war demands more effective preparedness.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that Canadians will be proud to play their full part once again in a United Nations operation which is designed to restore peace and prevent conflict spreading. But I do hope we will learn the lesson of these operations so that we will not have to work out these ad hoc arrangements on the spur of a crisis, that somehow the United Nations will work out an arrangement by which we will be ready for this kind of thing, and that not only Canada but all members of the United Nations will play their full part in international peace and security by preventing little conflicts from spreading to become big conflicts, which is perhaps the greatest danger we face in the world today. That danger at the moment is centering on Cyprus, and goodness knows what might happen if that danger is not removed.
I believe that this United Nations force, if it can get to Cyprus quickly, will play once again an essential part in removing this kind of danger and in the re-establishment of peace and security in this part of the world, just as such action has been successful in doing, in the past, in other parts of the

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we of the opposition have made our position perfectly clear on more than one occasion and it is not necessary this evening for me to go into any detail. Throughout the period since the establishment of the United Nations in 1945 we have taken the stand that a prime responsibility of responsible members of the United Nations is that each and all of us shall discharge our respective responsibilities to the United Nations, and thereby assure that institution's ability to carry out its objectives, its purposes and its aims.
I want to begin by referring to one matter that is of interest as one looks back over the years, and has to do with the fact that this resolution is brought before parliament. I recall that the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen in 1925 enunciated, as a principle for Canadian participation of troops abroad, that parliament should decide. That view was not generally accepted at the time. Many believed

that the principles that had existed a generation or so earlier were still in effect, and this action tonight is but one more step in the constitutional development and final establishment of the principle that we in this nation will not send our troops abroad without a decision by parliament.
In so far as the recital given by the Prime Minister is concerned, I can but say that the only facts I have are those that have been placed before parliament. It is one of the ironies of our situation that the course followed in the United Kingdom is not followed here, namely that those who have occupied the position of prime minister and others who have been privy councillors are generally made aware of the dispatches that are received so that they may be in a position to discuss with their supporters the principles that should be brought about, based on the information that is available to the leader of the party. I hope that in the future the government will do more than make a mere passing reference and will make available to those of Her Majesty's privy council the fullest of information. Certainly we are bound by our oath, and those who occupy the position of leadership of the opposition are certainly not going to reveal information that is made available to the members of the privy council in the government of the country at the moment.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) has mentioned the difficulties of the present situation. NATO is in serious danger. NATO has been challenged from within by the events of the last few months. NATO is again being weakened at this time by the dispute between Greece and Turkey. Both of these nations are allies of ours, and as such it is natural that Canada, with the reputation she has throughout the world, should be considered from the beginning as one country which might make a provision of this kind. We have done more than any other nation to assist the United Nations in peace keeping operations. No other nation in the United Nations has made the same contributions and sacrifices to the ideals of San Francisco. This fact is often forgotten.
The Prime Minister mentioned the various peace keeping operations in which we have engaged, from 1956 onward. He referred to Korea which was one facet of the operations within the United Nations, and he referred, too, to the operations in the Middle East, the Congo, India and in Kashmir. There is another reason why Canada should participate at this time, and that is that Cyprus is a commonwealth nation. I was present when Cyprus was admitted as a member of this family of nations. I feel that no other country within the commonwealth, outside of the United
Peace Keeping Force to Cyprus Kingdom, could make a better contribution to good will and to the re-establishment of order in that country than could we.
It is of interest, too, that the commanding officer will be a commonwealth officer. Mr. Speaker, the members of this party recognize the need for making a speedy response to the appeal of the United Nations for Canada to make a contribution to the peace keeping forces which are to be sent to Cyprus.
I hope no group in this house, even though its members may disagree with the idea of sending a peace force to Cyprus, will hold up a decision which it is apparent the house wishes to make, and which the great bulk of the Canadian people wants to make in order that Canada may make the kind of response which I think has to be made at this time if the authority of the United Nations is to be maintained in this present world situation.
I think the government is to be congratulated, that in spite of the speed which is necessary at this time parliament is being consulted, not only because the Prime Minister gave an assurance that he would consult parliament but because a vital principle is at stake; no citizen should be committed to any type of armed conflict without the consent of the elected representatives of the Canadian people.
I am also glad that Canada has not stopped to haggle about the question of money. I agree with what has been said by both the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition-that there ought to be a permanent world peace keeping force and that it ought

to be financed by all the nations on an equitable basis. But for us to stop and haggle about money at this particular time would, be a mistake. I am glad the government has indicated its willingness to send a peace keeping force and finance it, rather than haggle while the situation in Cyprus continues to deteriorate.
We need have no illusions about the problem the United Nations will face in Cyprus where a bloody civil war has been going on. The population there is 83 per cent Greek and 17 per cent Turkish and it is now apparent that the 1959 constitution is not working and that the veto power which was vested in the minority has virtually brought government administration to a standstill.
I think one should recognize that neither Greece nor Turkey has been entirely without blame in this situation. There has been a great deal of encouragement given, sometimes amounting to direct provocation, to promoting the racial dissension and bitterness which obtains in Cyprus. I only hope that we in Canada will take a look at what is happening in Cyprus and that some of our people who take very extreme positions, in both English speaking and French speaking Canada, will realize the end result of demagogic appeals to racial antagonism and racial bitterness and realize what they could bring about in this country.
The real need in Cyprus is, first of all, a peace keeping operation. Of equal importance is the appointing of a mediator who will work out a modus vivendi by which these two groups of Cypriots can live together in peace. It seems to me the action we are being called upon to take tonight is made necessary because of the danger that civil war in Cyprus may turn into a general war. When the United Nations was formed, intervention by a United Nations force was thought of mainly in terms of preventing an aggressor nation imposing its will upon its neighbour. But the Congo situation demonstrated that there are times when the United Nations must intervene even in a civil war. The danger at the moment is that what is now a local civil insurrection could spread, especially if Turkey and Greece decide to intervene. A war in the Balkans could have far reaching repercussions. The Soviet union has always looked with an eager eye upon the Black sea and the Dardanelles and if the United States and the Soviet union were to take opposite sides in the struggle between Greece and Turkey a war could be precipitated from which it would be difficult for Canada to remain aloof. In any war in which the United States and Russia were involved Canada would be a battleground, if not on land, then certainly, in the air.

Until now the people of Great Britain have borne the major responsibility for trying to restore peace in Cyprus. I think this parliament is being asked to take the only course which is open to it. I think a commonwealth force would have been impracticable, first because there is no central decision making body which could have taken day to day decisions, and also because a commonwealth force would have been associated in the public mind with Great Britain which was long a colonial power there, and would have been resented by the Cypriots. I think a NATO force would have been unwise. I do not believe NATO was set up to do this kind of job; it was set up to meet a special situation which we all think is gradually improving. Only the United Nations has the authority and the prestige to undertake the kind of intervention which could be effective in the present circumstances.
I want to say that in passing this motion neither we in this house nor the Canadian people ought to have any illusions about what we are doing. I think we have to recognize that we are assuming a hazardous, thankless and discouraging task. We have to be prepared for a long and difficult assignment in which lives may be lost. Moreover, the role we play may be an unpopular one. Nobody ever made friends by interfering in a family fight. I hope we recognize that this will be an arduous and a dangerous task and that we ought not to go into it without weighing all its aspects; we should go into it with our eyes open and our resolve high.
To those who object to Canada's contributing to this peace force I say: What is the alternative? The alternative is that we can do nothing. If we refuse to respond to the appeal of the United Nations and if other countries which have been invited also refuse to respond, we would sit back and almost certainly face the danger of war spreading in the Balkans and, quite possibly, throughout the world. This is one instance where an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. It is one instance where putting out a brush fire may prevent a major conflagration. Therefore, we in this party believe we have only one choice-that the only hope for world peace lies in maintaining the rule of law in the world.
We think that, ultimately, a permanent world police force financed by all the nations of the world on an equitable basis is the only solution. In the meantime, we must make ad hoc arrangements as was done in Suez, the Gaza strip, in the Congo and in Korea. Now, once more, we are making an ad hoc arrangement in order to meet a serious situation. We hope that some day not only will there be a stand-by permanent world police force but
Peace Keeping Force to Cyprus that we shall have legislation on our statute books so that we shall not have the scramble we have had in the last few days; so that the government will have the authority to act any time it is invited by the United Nations to despatch a peace keeping force to wherever the United Nations requires it to maintain law and order throughout the world. We do not have that at the present time. Therefore it seems to me that we must act now, and act quickly, to maintain the authority of the United Nations; because if the United Nations is not able to raise a peace keeping force at this time, its authority is gone-nations will disregard and ignore it, and it will become nothing but a debating society, without power, without authority and without a voice in world affairs.
Let us face the fact that in an assignment such as that upon which we are embarking, lives may be lost. In all probability lives will be lost, just as policemen every day in our respective communities risk their lives to maintain law and order. The Canadian people will have to appreciate the fact, as I am sure they will, that this is part of the price we must pay if we are to maintain the rule of law throughout the world. Because, Mr. Speaker, in this rapidly contracting world of the second half of the 20th century peace is indivisible; when peace is violated in any corner of the world, unless the situation is dealt with promptly peace will gradually be destroyed everywhere. If mankind is ever to see brought to fruition Tennyson's dream of "a parliament of man and a federation of the world", then nations such as Canada have to be prepared to make their contribution toward maintaining peace and order throughout the world.

I do not wish to dwell further on that point; besides, I know that my speech is of no avail, that I know, just as I know that I am speaking to persons who will openly laugh at my comments. I also know that tonight I speak for people in need, who will eventually come and ask for the same assistance that we are giving tonight to our friends in foreign countries.
Mr. Speaker, if there are people with a strong love for peace, we are those people;
[Mr. Gauthier.!

but let us start by giving food to those who are hungry and let us stop putting guns in the hands of those whose stomachs are empty. Those are the foundations of peace. I would be very happy to go without sleep for two nights if the Prime Minister presented a bill of this kind to help our farmers.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think that the people of Canada will wonder several days from now why there was this unusual haste, and why some of the things happened that are taking place tonight. Is this not an indication of our lack of planning and a need to do something in a much more formal and better way to deal with such a situation than is the case tonight? Certainly the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) is a long-time proponent of the idea of a peace force, and certainly if we had taken action like that taken by Norway, Sweden and Denmark in establishing a peace force for use by the United Nations any place in the world-

subsubtopic: KEEPING FORCE
speechtext: We already have.

subsubtopic: KEEPING FORCE
speechtext: We have, but we have done so in a very odd way. These countries have established such forces, and I am sure that if we had done so in the same way it would have led to the dispatch of troops in an orderly manner befitting our country.

subsubtopic: KEEPING FORCE
speechtext: That is in Europe.

subsubtopic: KEEPING FORCE
speechtext:
That may be so, but I think that the matter would have been handled in a much more dignified way than the way we are handling it now. Several methods have been used tonight that were used in the pipe line debate or in other exceptional cases. It seems to me that this is not the way to do these things. It seems to me that while we may have used the parliamentary system to accomplish something very worth while, at the same time we have done so in a way that degrades the whole system.
There is one point I want to raise having to do with the relationship of Canadian personnel who will be taking part in this peace corps operation. As the Prime Minister said, they will be going into a very serious situation, and certainly we are proud of the fact that Canadians are available to go and that we have the money to send them and are able to provide them with the necessary equipment required by their role. But I am wondering if it is not time for the Prime Minister to rise and say what protection is going to be afforded these troops.
I have been a member of the veterans affairs committee for some time, and we have been shocked by the lack of coverage and protection for our soldiers and other service

people in Europe. It seems that the same situation will apply as far as the troops going to Cyprus are concerned unless a specific change is made in this regard. I can give an example of an airman on a base in Germany who was told to bring his family to the base for inoculation because they might come in contact with other personnel who had been in an area where there had been an epidemic. When this airman drove his family back to the town where they were living, he was under orders to return to the base to finish his day's work, and on his way back he was killed by a truck. His wife and his family have been completely neglected. They have received no benefits, except what they were granted under an insurance policy, and they are now charges on the mother and father of the airman who was killed.
Every member of the veterans affairs committee knows that this is the situation with regard to our personnel, and I think the Prime Minister should rise and say that we are going to be fair to these troops who are going into an area of combat and will give them full coverage and all the benefits of the veterans charter. I believe that these troops are going to do a good job for us and I agree with all that has been said about this peace keeping mission. However, they are going into a theatre of war, and we should in return provide them with all the protection we have given to service personnel in other theatres of war in the past.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that before this resolution is adopted we should be assured that all the necessary protection for service personnel going into active service is given. No doubt, the Prime Minister will give us the assurance that this is going to be done. I think this is a case where you are not only going to be shot going forward but it will be a little bit like the poem which refers to "cannons to the right of them, cannons to the left of them, volleyed and thundered". It may be that serious. We should certainly make sure that these men who did not volunteer necessarily for war will not need to have any qualms at all about accepting the responsibility for which they have volunteered. We, in turn, should give them complete coverage that would be afforded to personnel in any theatre of war.

And if that came about, we owe it to the efforts made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) who went all out, offering the services of Canadians and making it possible for us to play our given part, that is to preserve peace throughout the world.
Mr. Speaker, even if I spoke harshly at times tonight, I assure you that I was not against the motion, but against the procedure that was followed. Incidents such as the ones which occurred tonight unavoidably lead to war. In fact, that may be how hostilities started in Cyprus, because citizens were unhappy with the policy followed by the authorities.
Anyhow, even if I disagree with some members of my party on that point-they are aware of my feelings as I am aware of theirs and we mutually respect each other's opinions -I am in favour of the motion introduced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) because I feel Canada has a role to play not only in Cyprus or in the Congo but everywhere in the world.
Canada must contribute to the restoration of peace and the prevention of war.
Moreover, as was pointed out a moment ago, Canada also has a role to play within its own territory, for we cannot overlook the fact that if people suffer today and will suffer tomorrow in Cyprus, there are also people in Canada who suffer.
Mr. Speaker, we cannot forget that there is hardship in Canada ( and I am well aware of it because I have witnessed it in my own riding. I hope that the action taken tonight, which springs from the desire of the Canadian people to help alleviate suffering in the world, will convince us to reduce suffering and misfortune throughout the world as well as in our country.
Mr. Speaker, I hope that the Prime Minister and the members of his cabinet will continue their efforts towards alleviating suffering and destitution everywhere, outside as well as inside our country.

subsubtopic: KEEPING FORCE
speechtext: If I may just answer that point, I would say that I believe Canadian governments have had a good reputation in relation to the treatment of their servicemen and their dependants. They have been treated equitably and, indeed generously. I can assure my hon. friend, and the hon. member who preceded him that Canadian troops who proceed, if they do, to this theatre of operation will be given the protection of Canadian forces on active service. If there are special circumstances which require special protection, I am sure the Department of National Defence will take that matter into consideration, including the remarks made by the hon. member a few minutes ago.

Consequential upon this resolution which we have adopted, I move:
That a message be sent to the Senate informing Their Honours that this house has adopted a resolution approving of the participation of Canadian forces in the United Nations international force in Cyprus, and requesting Their Honours to unite with this house in the approval of the same by filling up the blanks in the resolution with the words, "Senate and".
Motion agreed to.
